target_refs.quote: In the present case, it is not disputed that the premises had been let for residential purposes, but it is also beyond doubt that to the knowledge of the landlord the premises have been regularly used by the tenant not only for her own residence but also for her foreign guests.

element_targets.reason: The Supreme Court expressly accepted that the premises had been let for residential purposes. The frozen input independently contains the statutory authorities' prior finding that the premises had been let for residential purposes, so the input contains sufficient support for this condition. The later failure of the section 14(1)(e) ground does not invert this condition.

target_refs.quote: Assuming that the bona fide requirement of the landlord is established, the landlord must still prove that the premises had been let for residential purposes.

element_targets.reason: The Supreme Court expressly proceeded on an assumption that bona fide requirement was established rather than adjudicating that condition. The frozen input supplies no facts or prior finding concerning the landlord's bona fide residential requirement.

The Supreme Court did not substantively determine whether the claimed occupation was by the landlord herself or by a dependent family member. Its decisive reasoning concerned the residential-purpose characterization under the Explanation and the landlord's consent to the longstanding boarding-house use. The frozen input does not identify or support a qualifying occupation route.

target_refs.quote: The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964 and thus stepped into his shoes as the `landlord' as defined under section 2(e) of the Act.

element_targets.reason: The Supreme Court's accepted factual matrix states that the respondent purchased the property from the original landlord, supporting the ownership qualification. The frozen input, however, preserves only the respondent's relationship to the original landlord and the original letting; it omits the decisive purchase fact, so it is insufficient for this target.

The Supreme Court did not apply or determine the alternative route involving occupation by a person for whose benefit the premises were held. The frozen input contains no facts concerning such a person or such a holding arrangement.

The Supreme Court did not substantively determine whether the landlord or another qualifying person lacked other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. The reference near the end of the judgment to alternative accommodation concerns the separate case numbered 1870868, not this case, and the frozen input for case 1114159 supplies no accommodation evidence.

cases.procedural_outcome_separate: The Supreme Court allowed the tenant's appeal, set aside the Delhi High Court judgment, and restored the orders of the Additional Rent Controller dated 29 September 1976 and the Rent Control Tribunal dated 18 November 1978.
coverage_limits: The supplied GIVEN template omits the text and conditions of the statutory Explanation to section 14(1)(e), even though the Supreme Court's decisive reasoning turned on incidental commercial use, landlord knowledge, and implied consent under that Explanation.

The Court held that longstanding, open use as a boarding house with the landlord's knowledge and implied consent took the premises outside the relevant residential-purpose ambit for the eviction ground; that decisive consent issue is not one of the six GIVEN conditions and therefore is not converted into a substitute target.

The frozen input is retrospectively reconstructed and does not contain the purchase fact used for the ownership qualification or facts concerning bona fide need, occupation route, or alternative residential accommodation.
C01 remains SATISFIED even though the section 14(1)(e) eviction ground ultimately failed; condition polarity is not inverted to match the procedural outcome.

target_refs.quote: The appellant is the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent- landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954, evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year
We have already indicated that, under the Rent Act two grounds for eviction have been good by the landlord. Indisputably, sub-letting has been substantiated.

element_targets.reason: The tenancy itself began on 19 May 1954, after 9 June 1952, and the Supreme Court accepted that sub-letting by that tenant was substantiated. The relevant sub-letting therefore necessarily occurred after the statutory cutoff. The frozen input contains the 1954 letting date and the prior section 14(1)(b) sub-letting finding, making the timing condition sufficiently supported.

target_refs.quote: Arguments before us have proceeded on the footing that a sub-tenancy has been created and this amounts to a breach of condition with a provision for re-entry.

element_targets.reason: The Supreme Court expressly treated sub-letting as substantiated and proceeded on the footing that a sub-tenancy had been created. That is a substantive acceptance of the subletting route rather than merely a procedural dismissal. The frozen input contains the Appellate Tribunal's prior finding upholding sub-letting under section 14(1)(b), which is sufficient to expose this legal route even though the detailed underlying proof of each tenancy incident is not separately reproduced.

The Supreme Court adjudicated the case on the footing of sub-letting/sub-tenancy and did not determine that the tenant assigned and divested himself of all tenant rights. The frozen input likewise contains no assignment allegation or finding.

The Supreme Court did not separately adjudicate the alternative parting-with-possession route or find that the tenant divested or abandoned his own right to possession. The case was treated as one of substantiated sub-letting, and the frozen input contains no possession-divestment facts.

target_refs.quote: The Rent Controller, at the floor level, ordered eviction and the Appellate Tribunal affirmed it, upholding the vice of sub-letting without consent of the landlord in the manner specified in section 14(1)(b)
We have already indicated that, under the Rent Act two grounds for eviction have been good by the landlord. Indisputably, sub-letting has been substantiated.

Many other niceties of law were presented to us by Shri A. K. Sen to extricate the tenant from eviction. They are too unsubstantial and intricate for us to be deflected from the sure and concurrent findings, read in the background of an alternative accommodation being available to the tenant.

element_targets.reason: The judgment recounts the concurrent finding of sub-letting without the landlord's consent in the manner specified by section 14(1)(b), and the Supreme Court expressly treats the Rent Act ground as made out, calls sub-letting indisputably substantiated, and declines to depart from the concurrent findings. This constitutes adoption of the no-consent component. The frozen input contains the same Tribunal finding of sub-letting without consent under section 14(1)(b), so it is sufficient for this condition.

The qualification concerning concurrent use while the tenant retains legal possession belongs to the alternative parting-with-possession route. The Supreme Court did not analyze that route or decide whether the tenant retained concurrent legal possession. The frozen input contains no facts addressing concurrent use or retention of possession.

cases.procedural_outcome_separate: The Supreme Court dismissed the tenant's appeal and directed that the eviction order be executed only on or after 1 March 1976, with the parties bearing their own costs throughout.
coverage_limits: The Supreme Court expressly treated sub-letting as substantiated and adopted the concurrent findings, but the supplied judgment does not reproduce the detailed evidentiary record establishing each individual incident of the landlord-and-tenant relationship between tenant and sub-tenant.

For C02 and C05, input sufficiency rests on the frozen record's explicit Appellate Tribunal finding that sub-letting without consent under section 14(1)(b) had been upheld; the underlying testimonial or documentary proof of the sub-tenancy itself is not reproduced in the frozen input.
The assignment and parting-with-possession alternatives were not separately adjudicated and are therefore preserved as NOT_DECIDED rather than being inferred from the successful subletting route.

The Supreme Court's principal extended reasoning concerned determination of the lease, forfeiture, notice, and justice, equity and good conscience. Those issues are outside the six GIVEN section 14(1)(b) conditions and are kept separate from these element targets.
